# 3-parent papers

PSU DS 340W:
Three Papers, One Story
Lu Lin, Ph.D.

College of Information Sciences and Technology
Pennsylvania State University
lulin@psu.edu
Notes: Today we will connect the three paper-reading rounds to the methodology of your final scholarly paper. The goal is to leave with a focused improvement that your team can implement and evaluate.

# 3-parent papers

Give each parent paper a role
2
Paper | Primary role | What it contributes
Paper 1 | Anchor | Problem, dataset, task, or baseline
Paper 2 | Tension | Limitation, competing method, or unresolved issue
Paper 3 | Missing piece | Method, evaluation strategy, or supporting evidence
Sentence frame: Paper 1 establishes ____. Paper 2 shows that ____ remains a problem. Paper 3 suggests ____ as a way to address it.
Paper 3 should complete the project logic, not merely add another paper on the same topic.
Notes: The papers do not need equal roles. One may anchor the project, another may reveal the limitation, and the third may supply the missing technique or evaluation design. Ask students to say the sentence frame aloud.

# 3-parent papers

Possible contributions from Paper 3
Model: an algorithm, architecture, or component to adapt
Data pipeline: feature engineering, preprocessing, or missing-data handling
Learning strategy: class imbalance, regularization, sampling, or optimization
Experimental design: a stronger baseline, split strategy, or ablation
Evaluation: a metric for robustness, fairness, calibration, or interpretability
Scope: evidence that narrows the population, task, or conditions
3
A defensible adaptation or controlled combination can be a scholarly contribution. A new algorithm is not required.
Notes: Broaden students' definition of improvement. Better evaluation, robustness, interpretability, or handling of data problems may be more meaningful than a small increase in predictive accuracy.

# 3-parent papers

Synthesis matrix
4
Question | Paper 1 | Paper 2 | Paper 3 | Our decision
Research problem |  |  |  | 
Important limitation |  |  |  | 
Component to retain or change or improve |  |  |  | 
Evaluation (data, baselines, metric) |  |  |  | 
Main method |  |  |  | 
The final column converts reading into research/product decisions.
Notes: Do not accept three independent summaries as synthesis. Students should compare the papers across shared dimensions. The final column matters most because it states what the team will retain, reject, or modify.

# 3-parent papers

From literature to methodology
5
Observed
limitation
Evidence from
parent papers
One proposed
method change
Expected
effect
Controlled
experiment
Method statement: Because the papers show ____, we will modify ____ by ____. We will compare ____ using ____.
Notes: Walk from left to right. Every methodological choice should have a literature-based reason, and every claimed improvement should lead to an experiment that can support or reject it.

# 3-parent papers

One central methodological improvement
Identify one primary change and one main comparison.
Choose one primary outcome metric before running the experiment.
Keep supporting changes tied to the central idea.
Use an ablation when the proposed method contains multiple components.
6
BASELINE  +  ONE JUSTIFIED CHANGE  +  CONTROLLED COMPARISON
Notes: Changing the dataset, preprocessing, model, loss function, and evaluation at once prevents a clear conclusion. Supporting changes are acceptable, but they must serve one central methodological idea.

# 3-parent papers

Research question and hypothesis
7
Research question
Compared with [baseline], does [specific modification] improve [primary outcome] on [dataset or task]?
Hypothesis
We expect [method] to improve [metric] while maintaining [important constraint or secondary metric].
State what result would support the hypothesis and what result would not.
Notes: A useful research question names the baseline, the modification, the outcome, and the context. Ask students to define both success and failure before they see the results.

# 3-parent papers

Evaluation that isolates the contribution
8
Condition | Purpose
Original baseline | Provides the reference performance
Proposed method | Tests the complete improvement
Ablation or intermediate version | Identifies which component causes the change
Hold constant: data split, preprocessing, metrics, tuning budget, and random seeds whenever possible.
Report: variability, computation, tradeoffs, and failure cases, not only the best score.
Notes: The comparison must isolate the claimed contribution. Encourage teams to report variability and tradeoffs. A method that improves one metric while harming another may still be useful, but the paper must explain the tradeoff.

# 3-parent papers

Common weak proposals
9
Weak statement | Stronger direction
Paper 3 is about the same topic. | Name the exact methodological decision it informs.
We will combine all three models. | Explain the mechanism and include an ablation.
We will improve accuracy. | Choose a task-relevant primary metric and a baseline.
Our method is novel because these papers did not use it. | Make a bounded contribution claim supported by a broader literature search.
Notes: These are warning signs rather than automatic failures. Ask students to replace vague claims with a mechanism, comparison, and measure. Three parent papers alone cannot establish novelty across an entire field.

# 3-parent papers

Round 3 reflection
Explanation of what Paper 3 adds to Papers 1 and 2
A synthesis matrix comparing all three parent papers
One supported gap or limitation
A specific methodological change, research question, and hypothesis
A feasible evaluation plan with baseline, metrics, and ablation
10
One-sentence test: We will modify ____ by ____ because the papers indicate ____. We will compare ____ using ____.
Every design decision in the methodology needs a reason. The parent papers should supply much of that reason.
Notes: The submission should move from reading to a project decision. If a team cannot complete the one-sentence test clearly, the proposed methodology is not yet specific enough.

# Guide_to_write_paper (1)

A Practical Guide to Writing a Research Paper
Firstname1 Lastname1 * 1 Firstname2 Lastname2 * 1 2 Firstname3 Lastname3 3
Abstract
Write the abstract as one self-contained paragraph,
usually four to six sentences. Begin with the prob-
lem and explain why it matters. Next, identify the
specific limitation of existing approaches. State
the central idea of your method and the main rea-
son it should work. End with the evaluation set-
ting and the most important quantitative or qualita-
tive findings. Use concrete results when possible,
and avoid citations, unexplained abbreviations,
and claims that are not supported in the paper.
1. Introduction
Typical length: 1.5–2 pages.
The introduction develops the argument summarized in the
abstract. A reader should understand the problem, the re-
search gap, the proposed solution, and the evidence for the
paper’s claims without reading the rest of the paper. A
useful paragraph-level structure is:
Problem and importance. Define the problem precisely.
Explain who or what is affected and why solving the prob-
lem matters. Use evidence or a concrete example when
available.
Existing approaches. Summarize how prior work addresses
the problem. Focus on the main families of approaches
rather than listing papers one by one.
Research gap. Explain the limitation that remains. State
what current methods cannot do, under which conditions
they fail, or which requirement they leave unmet. This
paragraph should lead directly to the goal of your work.
Proposed approach. Present the main idea at a high level.
Explain the insight or evidence that motivates it, name the
major components, and state the purpose of each component.
*Equal contribution 1Department of XXX, University of YYY ,
Location, Country 2Company Name, Location, Country 3School
of ZZZ, Institute of WWW, Location, Country. Correspondence
to: Firstname1 Lastname1 <first1.last1@xxx.edu>, Firstname2
Lastname2 <first2.last2@www.uk>.
Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine
Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025. Copyright 2025
by the author(s).
Give enough detail for readers to form a mental model
before they reach the method section.
Evidence and contributions. Briefly describe the evalua-
tion setting, including its scale and the dimensions being
tested, such as predictive quality, robustness, or efficiency.
Report the main findings with meaningful numbers and ex-
plain which claims they support. End with a concise list of
the paper’s specific contributions if that list helps readers
distinguish them.
Keep the story consistent across the abstract, introduction,
method, and evaluation. Each limitation introduced here
should motivate a design choice, and each major claim
should be tested later in the paper.
2. Related Works
Typical length: 0.5–0.75 page.
The related-work section positions your contribution within
the research literature. It expands the introduction’s discus-
sion of prior approaches and the research gap. Organize
the literature by subproblem, assumption, or technical ap-
proach rather than describing one paper at a time. Within
each group, synthesize the common ideas, note important
differences, and explain how your work relates to them.
Use citations for factual claims about earlier methods. Be
fair and precise: describe the settings in which prior ap-

Guide to Writing an Research Paper
3. Methodology
Typical length: about 2.5 pages.
The method section gives the technical details needed to
understand and reproduce the proposed approach. It expands
the high-level description in the introduction. Present the
material from general to specific, and use consistent notation
throughout.
3.1. Background and Problem Formulation
Define the task, inputs, outputs, notation, and assumptions.
Introduce only the established techniques needed to under-
stand your method, and cite their original sources. Make a
clear distinction between prior techniques and your contri-
butions.
3.2. Approach Overview
Give readers a concise view of the complete pipeline before
describing individual components. A diagram can help
when the method has several stages or interacting modules.
Explain what information moves between components and
what each component is designed to achieve.
3.3. Proposed Method
Replace this heading with the name of your approach and
add subsections as needed. For each component, explain its
purpose, inputs, operations, and outputs. State how the com-
ponent addresses a limitation identified in the introduction.
Define every symbol near its first use, specify objectives and
algorithms precisely, and distinguish design choices from
implementation details.
After writing the section, check that an informed reader
could implement the method without guessing important
steps.
4. Evaluation
Typical length: about 2.5 pages.
The evaluation should test the paper’s main claims rather
than merely report many results. Begin by turning each
claim into a clear research question. Then choose datasets,
baselines, metrics, and analyses that answer those questions.
4.1. Experimental Setup
Describe the following information clearly enough for read-
ers to assess and reproduce the experiments:
• datasets, data splits, preprocessing, scale, and relevant
statistics;
• baselines and why each one is an appropriate compari-
son;
• evaluation metrics, including definitions for unfamiliar
metrics and whether higher or lower values are better;
• model and pipeline configurations, training procedures,
hyperparameters, and selection criteria;
• hardware, software, runtime, and the number of ran-
dom seeds or repeated trials when these details affect
the results.
Use the same information and tuning budget for comparable
methods whenever possible. Explain any deviations. Re-
port variability or uncertainty when results may depend on
randomness, sampling, or measurement error.
4.2. Main Results
State the question that the experiment answers before pre-
senting the results. Introduce each table or figure in the
text, explain the main pattern, and connect that pattern to a
claim from the introduction. Do not repeat every number
in a table. Emphasize meaningful comparisons, including
absolute values as well as percentage improvements when
they aid interpretation.
4.3. Ablation and Analysis
Use ablations to test whether the proposed components con-
tribute as intended. Include diagnostic analyses that explain
when the method succeeds or fails. Depending on the pa-
per’s claims, useful analyses may examine robustness, sensi-
tivity to hyperparameters, data scale, computational cost, or
behavior across subgroups. Report negative or mixed results
when they change how the method should be understood.
4.4. Additional Experiments
Replace this heading with a description of the question being
tested. Apply the same pattern: state the goal, define the
comparison and metrics, present the evidence, and explain
what the result supports or limits.
5. Conclusion and Future Work
Write one concise paragraph that restates the problem, sum-
marizes the proposed approach, and reports the main find-
ings. State the most important limitation honestly and iden-
tify a specific direction for future work that follows from
it. Do not introduce new methods, results, or unsupported
claims in the conclusion.
